content: The Jerusalem cherry, scientifically known as Solanum pseudocapsicum, is a plant that belongs to the Solanaceae family, the same family as the deadly nightshade. Its fruit is toxic and should not be consumed. This plant is often cultivated as a decorative houseplant, but in certain regions of Australia, it has become an invasive weed. The Jerusalem cherry is a perennial plant that thrives in USDA hardiness zones up to zone 8. It is native to Peru and has the ability to withstand frost and cold weather conditions. These plants typically have a lifespan of up to 10 years. They begin producing fruit in their second or third year of growth and continue to bear fruit annually thereafter. The fruit of the Jerusalem cherry closely resembles cherry tomatoes in both taste and texture, as they share the same genus (Solanum) with tomatoes. This similarity can lead to confusion, but it is important to note that the fruit of the Jerusalem cherry is toxic. The primary toxic compound in Solanum pseudocapsicum is solanocapsine, an alkaloid that is chemically similar to other toxic alkaloids found in the same genus, such as solanine and atropine. While the toxin is poisonous, it is generally not life-threatening. However, ingestion of the fruit can result in gastrointestinal symptoms, including vomiting and gastroenteritis.
